caption: Figure 1: Comparison with other real-time object detectors, our proposed methods achieve state-of-the-arts performance.
description:
## Description
This is a line graph comparing the performance of various object detection models. The x-axis represents the V100 batch 1 inference time in milliseconds, while the y-axis shows the Average Precision (AP). The graph includes six series: YOLOv7, YOLOR, PPYOLOE, YOLOX, Scaled-YOLOv4, and YOLOv5 (r6.1). YOLOv7 is the highest performing model, followed by YOLOR, PPYOLOE, YOLOX, Scaled-YOLOv4, and YOLOv5. YOLOv7 is noted to be +120% faster.

## Text in figure
YOLOv7 (ours), YOLOR, PPYOLOE, YOLOX, Scaled-YOLOv4, YOLOv5 (r6.1), better, better, AP, V100 batch 1 inference time (ms), YOLOv7 is +120% faster

caption: Figure 2: Extended efficient layer aggregation networks. The proposed extended ELAN (E-ELAN) does not change the gradient transmission path of the original architecture at all, but use group convolution to increase the cardinality of the added features, and combine the features of different groups in a shuffle and merge cardinality manner. This way of operation can enhance the features learned by different feature maps and improve the use of parameters and calculations.
description:
This figure is a diagram comparing four different network architectures: VoVNet, CSPVoVNet, ELAN, and E-ELAN. Each panel shows the structure of the network, with blocks and layers labeled. The networks use various techniques to increase feature cardinality and improve parameter efficiency. VoVNet and CSPVoVNet use cross-stage connections, while ELAN and E-ELAN use stack-in-computational blocks. E-ELAN introduces group convolution to further enhance feature learning.

Text in figure: VoVNet, CSPVoVNet, ELAN, E-ELAN, cross-stage connection, stack-in-computational block, expand cardinality, shuffle cardinality, merge cardinality, 3x3, 2x2, 4c, 8c, 2c, 1x1.

caption: Figure 3: Model scaling for concatenation-based models. From (a) to (b), we observe that when depth scaling is performed on concatenation-based models, the output width of a computational block also increases. This phenomenon will cause the input width of the subsequent transmission layer to increase. Therefore, we propose (c), that is, when performing model scaling on concatenationbased models, only the depth in a computational block needs to be scaled, and the remaining of transmission layer is performed with corresponding width scaling.
description:
This figure is a diagram illustrating different scaling methods for concatenation-based models in neural networks. It shows three panels: (a) a concatenation-based model, (b) a scaled-up concatenation-based model with increased depth, and (c) a compound scaling method that adjusts both depth and width. The diagram highlights how scaling up depth affects the width of computational blocks and subsequent transmission layers.

Text in figure: concatenation-based model, scaled-up concatenation-based model, compound scaling, computational block, transition, scaling up depth, scaling up width, partial scaling up width, cross stage merge.

caption: Figure 4: Planned re-parameterized model. In the proposed planned re-parameterized model, we found that a layer with residual or concatenation connections, its RepConv should not have identity connection. Under these circumstances, it can be replaced by RepConvN that contains no identity connections.
description:
This figure is a diagram showing different types of convolutional layers used in neural network architectures. It includes PlainNet, RepPlainNet, ResNet, RepResNet, P1-RepResNet, P2-RepResNet, P3-RepResNet, and P4-RepResNet. Each type is represented by a series of blocks labeled with "Conv" or "RepConv" and "RepConvN". The figure highlights the importance of not using identity connections in layers with residual or concatenation connections, suggesting the use of RepConvN instead.

Text in figure: PlainNet, RepPlainNet, ResNet, RepResNet, P1-RepResNet, P2-RepResNet, P3-RepResNet, P4-RepResNet, 3x3 Conv, RepConv, RepConvN, Conv, c, ✓, ✗.

caption: Figure 5: Coarse for auxiliary and fine for lead head label assigner. Compare with normal model (a), the schema in (b) has auxiliary head. Different from the usual independent label assigner (c), we propose (d) lead head guided label assigner and (e) coarse-to-fine lead head guided label assigner. The proposed label assigner is optimized by lead head prediction and the ground truth to get the labels of training lead head and auxiliary head at the same time. The detailed coarse-to-fine implementation method and constraint design details will be elaborated in Apendix.
description:

It shows five different models: (a) Normal model, (b) Model with auxiliary head, (c) Independent assigner, (d) Lead guided assigner, and (e) Coarse-to-fine lead guided assigner. Each model has a different approach to assigning labels to the lead and auxiliary heads during training.

caption: Figure 9: Comparison with other object detectors.
description:
This figure is a line graph comparing the performance of various object detectors on the MS COCO mini-val dataset. It plots the Average Precision (AP) percentage against the V100 batch=1 inference time in milliseconds. The YOLOv7 series is highlighted with a red line, showing it is the fastest and most accurate. YOLOv7-E6E has the highest AP at 56.80%, while YOLOv7-tiny-SILU has the lowest at 38.70%. The graph also includes other detectors like PPYOLEO, YOLOX, YOLOR, YOLOv5, and Transformers.
